facts.format: Lecture 1: Data Foundations and SQL Intro. 120 minute class plus 30 minutes of doubts. Hour 1, orientation, 60 minutes: opening hook 10, what is DSML 8, the 3 career tracks 7, why SQL now 10, FOMO demo 10, expectations and the 20-minute rule 6, think like an analyst 4 (paired activity), then a 5 minute break. Hour 2, technical foundations, 55 minutes: what is a database 8, DBMS 4, database vs Excel 7, database vs data warehouse 7, BigQuery and the first SQL query 7, your journey and close 5, practice preview 4.
facts.warm_up: The first 5 minutes are informal and unscripted: greet the learners, ask them to drop city, background (tech or non-tech) and one sport they like in chat, read 3 or 4 replies and react naturally. Then a 2 minute instructor introduction: [[FROM_SME: instructor name, years in the data space, LinkedIn]]. Say 'I have been exactly where you are: confused about where to start, what matters and what does not.' Drop the LinkedIn link in chat.
facts.opening_hook: The noise problem: learners hear 'AI will take jobs', 'you must learn AI', 'SQL is outdated'. Most are not confused because they cannot learn but because there is too much information and not enough direction. Ask how many come from a non-tech background and have found learning messy before: very normal. Analogy: five people giving five different routes confuse you, one clear route (first this, then this) is easy to follow. This program aims for simple, structured, step by step.
facts.what_is_dsml: DSML is the skill of turning raw, messy information into decisions that make money or save money. Flow: raw data (orders, payments, logs), analysis (SQL, Python, AI), insights (charts, dashboards), decision (a business action). Cricket analogy for 3 roles: scorecard analyst is the Data Analyst ('Virat scored 78 off 54, 60% of his runs came in the last 5 overs', looking backwards); team selector is the Data Scientist (predicts from his last 10 matches against pace in Dubai); DRS and Hawk-Eye is the AI or ML Engineer (a built system tracking 1200 frames per second). You cannot build Hawk-Eye without understanding the scorecard, so we start with the scorecard.
facts.three_career_tracks: Data Analyst understands the past (which city had the most cancellations last week); Data Scientist predicts the future (which customer will cancel next month); AI or ML Engineer builds the automated system (a recommendation engine for 20 million users). Weak foundation means wrong predictions means failing systems, so the foundation comes first. Whatever role a learner picks, the starting path is the same: Data Analytics, SQL first.
facts.dashboard_walkthrough: Recorded Scaler dashboard walkthrough: https://www.loom.com/share/b01d23737d4a4193a37aab23a941d72b . It covers navigating the dashboard, accessing courses, assessments and study materials, and tracking progress and performance. If time permits share it with learners; it is also a pre-read on their dashboard.
facts.why_sql_now: AI did not kill SQL, it made SQL more valuable. What AI does well: writes syntax, suggests structure, explains a query. Where AI needs you: business context, deciding the right question, checking the answer. Where SQL is irreplaceable: running on actual company data, returning verifiable numbers, being auditable (the SQL is the receipt). Line to land: AI writes the syntax, you own the question. The 2026 analyst workflow: a business question arrives; translate it into a precise ask; you and AI write the SQL together; run it on the company database (only you have access); sense-check the numbers (does revenue per city sum to the total, are NULLs handled); present the answer with the SQL attached.
facts.fomo_demo: Scene: you are a Zomato analyst at 9am Monday; the manager says orders dropped 22% in Bangalore last Saturday and wants answers by 11am. The pipeline: 1 extract Saturday's Bangalore orders against the previous 4 Saturdays (SQL on BigQuery); 2 find the dip by hour (SQL and Python); 3 diagnose by asking AI what could cause a 7 to 11 pm drop (Claude or ChatGPT); 4 visualise orders by hour against the 4-week average (Tableau or Power BI); 5 present: '22% drop, 7 to 11 pm, Swiggy promo in the same window, counter-offer within 48 hours'. Ask which part excites learners most and take 2 or 3 answers. Close: companies do not pay for step 1 alone, they pay for the whole answer.
facts.expectations_and_20_minute_rule: Success is practice, not intelligence. What works: attend every class or watch the recording the same day, write queries yourself, ask doubts publicly, build a portfolio as you go. What does not: passive watching, waiting to understand 100% before starting, skipping assignments, comparing your pace with others. The 20-minute rule: 20 minutes of practice every single day; 20 times 180 days is 60 hours in 6 months, more than most people clock in a year. By the end of the module learners will write complex SQL on a real company database independently, use AI tools to accelerate analysis and catch when AI is wrong, explain business problems through data, and walk into interviews with a portfolio.
facts.think_like_an_analyst: Chat activity: Zomato orders dropped 22% last Saturday across all cities; you have 2 hours to explain why; what do you check and why? The instructor guides and does not correct. Senior checklist: app performance (crashes, slow loads), weather across cities, competitor promotion (a 50% off the same evening), pricing or delivery fee changes, holiday or big event (an IPL final). Junior says 'orders dropped 22%'; senior says 'dropped 22%, concentrated 7 to 10 pm in Tier-1 cities, correlates with a competitor's 50% off campaign, counter-promote next Saturday in the same slot'.
facts.hour_2_analogies: Ask first: how many ordered on Zomato, and where does that data go? Database as the IRCTC railway reservation system (your PNR and seat go into a live, structured, searchable table; the TC checking your ticket is a query; most-booked routes is SQL). Database as the bank vault, DBMS as the teller, SQL as what you say to the teller: database stores, DBMS governs, SQL is how you talk to it. Database as the kitchen (live, cooking now) versus data warehouse as the recipe book (historical, for learning). BigQuery as Google Docs for data: no install, just a browser.
facts.database_content: A database is an organised collection of data you can search very quickly. Why databases exist: volume (50 customers vs 5 million), consistency (USA, United States, us), multiple users editing at once, complex questions (orders above 500 rupees in Bangalore last week by payment method). A database system: data, DBMS, schema (the blueprint), queries. Writing, reading, updating (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and keeping things consistent (all steps succeed or none). Types: relational (SQL), NoSQL (MongoDB), cloud databases (BigQuery). DBMS examples: MySQL (Flipkart, Swiggy, most web backends), PostgreSQL (startups), BigQuery (what we use), Snowflake (large companies). Database vs Excel: Excel struggles above 1 million rows, a database handles 10 billion; email-file version chaos vs one live source; manual vs automatic updates; file-wide access vs role-based access; minutes vs seconds; manual work vs scheduled queries. Excel is a tool, SQL is a skill, you need both but SQL gets you hired. Database vs data warehouse: live operational data vs historical data; apps vs analysts; insert, update, delete, read vs mostly read; MySQL and PostgreSQL vs BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift.
facts.bigquery_and_first_query: BigQuery is Google's cloud data tool, free to start, no download, at console.cloud.google.com. Setup is homework tonight: a step-by-step document https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xSeFZPm8rL4CQSwEp9nsJOmqG89YrGXY/view?usp=sharing and a Loom video are in the class group. First query, read like English: SELECT * FROM zomato.customers WHERE city = 'Bangalore'; meaning give me everything from the customers table, only for people in Bangalore. WHERE is covered properly in later lectures. Line to land: in 15 lectures you will write queries 3 times as complex without thinking.
facts.close_and_practice: Journey close: learners walk out knowing what a database is and why it exists, the database vs data warehouse difference in one sentence, the Zomato schema (two tables, one bridge, customer_id), and what a SQL query looks like. Practice preview: for five business questions, which Zomato table would you look at first (customers signed up in January 2024, payment method that fails most, Prime members in Pune, average order value last Saturday, cities with the slowest delivery).
facts.quiz_pattern: Five multiple choice quizzes, one after each of the sections: what is a database, DBMS, database vs Excel, database vs data warehouse, first SQL query. Each has four options, the correct answer, and an explanation. Example: in the query SELECT * FROM zomato.customers WHERE city = 'Bangalore', the star means everything, all columns.
facts.section_bridges: Every section ends with a two or three sentence spoken bridge that connects it to the next one (for example from the 20-minute rule to the analyst challenge: before we touch code, can you think like a pro).
